en.text: Look at what they assert: the order things were called in, that the contract received both stacks, and that each side got its role with the same contract and the same story embedded. Not one check on whether what was generated is any good, because that isn't its call. The rest of the file is two more lines — that it returns the files — and a second three-line test: that it rejects an empty user story. That's all of it.

Now try writing the test for that smart version. What do you assert? Not the order, because the order is no longer fixed: it depends on what it decides on each run. Not the content, because that changes every time you run it. What you're left with is something like "check that the decision was a good one", and that isn't an assertion: it's an opinion shaped like code. That's the difference, and it isn't a matter of taste: you can assert on structure; judgment, at best, you can evaluate. chalc itself keeps the two verbs apart: the deterministic part has ordinary tests, and the part that touches AI has its own command, `chalc eval-ia`, which runs local evaluations of the prompts and parsers without calling the provider. It isn't the same guarantee: a test tells you "this always holds"; an evaluation gives you a score over a sample. The more a piece decides, the more of your confidence moves from the first category to the second.
Two consequences follow from that, and both are practical:

items: **What isn't tested doesn't warn you when it breaks.** The day that smart version starts deciding worse — because I switched models, because the provider updated theirs, because I touched a line of the prompt — no test goes red. You find out from the result, three repos downstream.

**And no test would catch its mistakes.** Tests defend the contract: if a lane builds something different from what the paper says, its test fails and gives it away. But that only works if the paper is right. Imagine chalc is the one deciding and it decides wrong: it puts in the contract that the second cancellation returns 200. All three lanes implement it as written, all three write their tests against that rule, and all three stay green — the error is in the rule, and the tests only check that the rule is followed. That's why I approve the contract before it flows down to any lane: I'm the only filter that reviews the rule itself, not its compliance.

**And it would have to know all three stacks at once.** To hold an opinion on the mobile lane you need Dart and how a widget test works; for the web, Angular. Packing all three into one head is precisely the opposite of what makes this work — which is what the rest of this section is about: each lane receiving only its own.

en.caption: Both designs have the same shape and differ in exactly one thing: what sits at the centre. On the left, decisions that only exist inside a model's output. On the right, a file you can open, review and approve.

en.text: Notice what I'm not saying, because it's easy to take this to the opposite extreme: I'm not saying decisions are unnecessary. There are decisions to make, plenty of them — which fields the response carries, what happens when you cancel twice, whether the token expires. What I'm saying is where they have to live. A smart chalc would make them and leave them inside its own output, where nobody reviews them because nobody knows they're there. Mine pushes them up into the contract: a fingerprinted file I read and approve before it reaches any lane. The decision doesn't disappear, it moves — and by moving it goes from invisible to being a diff.

And what do I lose? Something real, and I'd rather say it: a smart `chalc` could smell that the web and mobile are about to read the same 409 differently before it happens. Mine doesn't see that, because it never looks inside any lane. That job stays with me — reading the contract before approving it — and the contract itself hands part of it back when it flags what's missing as `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` instead of filling it in on its own. It's slower than a clever machine. It's also the only version where I know who decided what.

But it's very easy to draw a false conclusion from that: that chalc therefore rules over nothing. It does rule over something, and it's precisely the thing that matters. It doesn't decide how each lane codes, but it does decide which rules apply in each lane, and it hands them over equipped before anyone writes a line. That's the difference between telling someone how to do their job — unnecessary — and giving them the house manual before they start — essential.
And it doesn't hand everyone the same thing, because not everyone does the same thing. This is what reaches each lane:

items: **The contract**, identical in all three repos: `contracts/api.md`, with the endpoints, the models, the authentication and the requirements in EARS notation (`WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …`).

**Its spec, and only its own**, with the role written inside: the backend knows it exposes the API; the web and the mobile app know they consume it, and are forbidden from reimplementing backend logic.
**The same requirement identifiers.** R2 is R2 in all three repos: it isn't renumbered per lane, because renumbering loses cross-repo traceability and then you can't search for anything.

**Its skills, which are not the same for everyone.** Angular gets its 14 — signals, http, routing, testing, responsive design…; Nest gets its best-practices one; Flutter gets its 8 — widgets, state, navigation, async, performance, testing.

**Its MCP server**: `angular-cli` on the web, `dart` on mobile, `postgres` optionally on the backend. Each lane queries its live documentation instead of the version the model remembers from training.
**And the shared standard, which isn't negotiable**: clean code, minimal implementation, SOLID, modular architecture and mutation testing. Every repo inherits those five, whatever the stack.

lines: →        skills: 14 angular ones + the 5 global ones · mcp: angular-cli
→        skills: 8 flutter ones + the 5 global ones · mcp: dart
→ method in all three: spec-driven development ✓

en.caption: At the top, what every repo inherits no matter what. Below, what belongs to each lane. chalc hands this out and steps aside: what you write with it is your business.

en.text: There's a detail that sounds minor and isn't: that detection isn't done by an AI. `chalc` looks at project signals — a dependency declared in `package.json`, a `pubspec.yaml` at the root — and applies explicit rules from its catalog. It's instant, it gives the same result every time, and it costs not a single token. The piece that hands out the rules is the most boring one in the whole flow, and that's exactly why it's the only one that has never failed me.
The flow, start to finish

Put together and in order, this is how a feature starts. I come in with the user story, run `chalc feature`, and the first thing it does is ask me for the paths: the web, the backend and, if the feature has an app, the mobile one (via the `--mobile` flag or by asking me). From there it doesn't ask me anything else until the end.

items: It asks for the paths and detects each stack. It shows them to me — `Front: Angular · Back: NestJS · Mobile: Flutter` — so I can confirm it recognized each repo correctly **before** spending a token. If it got one wrong, I stop here instead of in the spec.
It prepares the ground: pulls each repo, checks whether the tree is clean, and equips it with its skills, its MCP and the method. This costs no tokens; they are catalog rules.

It generates the contract from the story: shared requirements in EARS (`WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …`), endpoints, models and errors. Whatever the story doesn't say isn't invented: it's flagged `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]`.
It specifies the backend against that already-closed contract, then the web and then the mobile app, both against the SAME contract. Each side gets its role written inside, and only its own part.

It seals: the same `specs/NNN-…` folder in every repo, the same R#, an identical copy of `contracts/api.md` in each spec, the contract fingerprint stamped into every file, and a `contract.lock.json` saved.
It creates the branch `feat/<slug>` in every repo or in none. If any of them had uncommitted changes, it creates it nowhere and tells me: I'd rather it do nothing than leave me half a feature.
And its last act: it prints a prompt and exits. That is where chalc ends.

en.text: The hand-off: the prompt with the paths where chalc steps aside

That final prompt is the piece it took me longest to see as a piece, because it looks like a farewell message from the console and it's actually the artifact connecting the two halves of the flow. It isn't a nice summary of what happened: it's an operating instruction, with each repo's absolute path inside, ready to paste into the agent. This is what it prints, undressed:

lines: You are the ORCHESTRATOR of this full-stack feature. You coordinate THREE repos
around a single API contract, with SDD and strict TDD.
📜 Contract (source of truth, identical in the specs): contracts/api.md
Every endpoint, request/response and error comes from there — invent nothing outside it.
- BACKEND (exposes the API):  D:/orders-api   → spec: specs/012-orders/
- FRONTEND (consumes the API): D:/orders-web  → spec: specs/012-orders/
- MOBILE (consumes the API):   D:/orders-app  → spec: specs/012-orders/
1. Start with the BACKEND (it owns the contract). Read its contracts/api.md,
specs/constitution.md and spec.md (R1, R2… in EARS). Follow plan.md and execute
tasks.md ONE task at a time. Implement EXACTLY the contract's endpoints.
2. Then the FRONTEND, but CONSUMING the contract (same routes/shapes);
3. Then the MOBILE app, consuming the SAME contract; don't reimplement backend
4. R# are SHARED: the same R# is satisfied on backend, frontend and/or mobile.
5. Per task, strict TDD: failing test (Red) → minimum code (Green) → refactor.
6. Before each task, state which R# and which repo; when done, stop and wait for my OK.
8. If something is [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] in the contract or a spec, ask me first.
The spec is the source of truth: if scope changes, update spec and contract first.

en.text: Look at point 8, because it's the one that closes the loop with everything above. It doesn't say "if you're missing something, sort it out". It says that anything needing to change enters through the contract and goes through me. It's the same rule I described at the start — a lane never asks anything of another lane — but written where it actually counts: inside the instructions the one writing the code is about to read, not in a README nobody opens.
A prompt isn't the CLI's goodbye: it's the one place where the rules reach whoever has to follow them, at the exact moment they're about to start.
That is where orchestration starts: one task, one failing test, and a stop

I paste that prompt into the agent and that's where the authority changes hands. Up to this point everything was done by a deterministic CLI; from here on a model works inside a loop, and **the orchestrator is it**, not chalc. The first line of the message says so literally: "You are the ORCHESTRATOR of this full-stack feature". All chalc did was leave the ground prepared and spell out how the game is played.
And orchestrating here isn't a vague metaphor, it's a turn with fixed steps. This is what the agent does, task by task:

items: **It reads before touching anything**: the contract, the project's constitution and its lane's spec, plus the skills chalc left equipped in that repo. It doesn't start from a blank page or from what it remembers from training.

**It announces the task**: it states which R# it's about to satisfy and in which repo, taken from `tasks.md`. Just one. This looks like bureaucracy and it's what lets me stop it in time: if it's going after the wrong requirement, I see it before it writes anything.
**It writes the failing test** and checks that it actually fails. A test that passes on the first run isn't testing what you think: usually it's testing that the code exists.
**It writes the minimum code** that turns it green. No jumping ahead to the next three requirements because "while I'm here".
**It refactors and runs the mutants.** If the score drops below the threshold, the task isn't done even with all tests green.
**It stops and waits for my OK.** It doesn't chain tasks on its own. This is where I review, and where I steer it back if it went the wrong way.

en.caption: The full turn. Note the two things the agent doesn't choose: the order of the lanes, which comes from the prompt, and the stop at the end of every task. And the red path: when it's missing something, it doesn't cross into the lane next door.

en.text: The order between lanes isn't its call either: the prompt tells it to start with the backend, because that's the contract's owner, and then move to the web to consume it without reimplementing its logic. And mobile shows up in that same prompt as a third consumer, with its repo and its spec; that part I hand to Codex, which works it in its own repo with the same `contracts/api.md` in front of it. Both agents orchestrate, each its own part, and neither knows the other exists.

And here it may look like I'm contradicting myself — earlier I said chalc decides nothing, and now I'm saying the agent decides — so it's worth laying the split out cleanly, because each decision has a different owner. **The WHAT is mine**: what the feature does, which endpoints exist, what happens when you cancel twice. It's in the contract, and I'm the one who approves the contract. **The HOW is the agent's**: which service to create, how to model the state, where validation goes, which widget to use. That's its job and it's right that it does it — inside its stack's rules, one task per turn, and with a stop in front of me at the end of each one. **And chalc decides neither**: it prepares the ground and hands out the roles. Three pieces, three roles, and none steps on the next one's.
The distributed team: two agents, one lane each

The fastest way I have to explain this part is to think of it as hiring. Imagine you build the team with people from different countries: each with their own rate, their own hours and their own way of working. That, on its own, isn't a problem. It only becomes one if each of them ships whatever they feel like. What makes a distributed team work isn't everyone being the same, it's everyone signing the same delivery and following the same standard. From there on, who each person is and what they cost becomes logistics.

With agents I do exactly that. Today Codex takes the mobile lane, in Flutter, and Claude Code takes the web in Angular and the backend in Nest. It isn't that one is better than the other in the abstract: it's a split with concrete reasons, and I'd rather state them as they are.

items: **Cost and usage limits.** Each tool has its cap. If I put all three lanes on one of them, I end up stuck mid-afternoon waiting for it to reset. Split up, both lanes move at once and neither runs into the other's limit.

**I'm testing them.** I want to see how each behaves on its own stack, with the same rules and the same contract in front of it. I don't yet have a conclusion I could defend with data, so I'm not going to write one here: for now it's a test in progress, not a verdict.

**One agent, one language.** The one on Flutter thinks in Dart and widgets for the whole session; the one on Angular and Nest thinks in TypeScript. Neither switches context halfway, which is exactly where focus goes and patterns start getting mixed.

**Each starts with its own context.** Claude Code reads the repo's `CLAUDE.md` and its skills in `.claude/skills/`; Codex reads `AGENTS.md`. Different files in different repos: neither carries the other's noise.

en.text: And how does each assistant receive its configuration? Because `chalc`'s targets are adapters: each one is a file that translates the same neutral catalog into its assistant's format — Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor and Gemini CLI. For Codex, that's the `AGENTS.md` plus its MCP servers in `.codex/config.toml`: the same skills and the same method as the rest, written in its format. That's the point of keeping the catalog neutral: adding a new assistant means writing one more adapter, not rethinking anything.

en.caption: Two agents, one lane each, and a wall in between: neither sees the other's repo. The only things crossing that wall are the contract, the R# and the shared standard.

en.text: A distributed team doesn't work because everyone works the same way, but because everyone delivers against the same thing. With agents it's identical: it doesn't matter which one writes the code if both answer to the same contract.
Tests were never optional; with an agent they're also the only evidence

When I code, a test is a safety net: it warns me the day I break something by accident. When an agent writes the code, the test stops being a net and becomes the only evidence that what was delivered is what was asked for. And it's worth saying when this happens, because it isn't an unavoidable flaw of the model: it happens when you let it run loose, with no contract, no spec and no test holding it. Loose, a model doesn't fail the way people fail. It doesn't hand you something visibly half-finished: it fills in what it doesn't know with whatever seems right to it, and hands it over complete, tidy, well named and compiling. Everything we use to judge code at a glance — that it reads well, that it looks right — stays flawless even when the substance is wrong. The reins in this flow exist precisely for that.
A loose agent doesn't produce code that looks suspicious. It produces code that looks good. That's why "I read it and it seems fine" stopped being a review.

That's where the method's rule comes from: the test goes first and has to fail before a single line of implementation exists. With an agent in front of you that isn't ceremony, it's the only thing that works. A test written **before** is a specification: it states what must happen, and the agent can't argue with it. A test written **after** is a description: it reports whatever the code does, whatever that is. Ask an agent to implement and then test, and it will write you a passing test — every time — because it writes it while looking at its own code. You'll have paid twice for the same opinion.

That's why the prompt requires confirming the red before moving on. Writing the test isn't enough: you have to watch it fail. A test that passes on the first run is almost never testing what you think; usually it's testing that the function exists and returns something. It's the quietest failure there is, and with three repos it multiplies without anyone noticing.
And why unit tests, and to a defined pattern

Unit tests first, for a practical reason: they're the only ones you can run in the second after writing them. The agent's cycle is write, run, look, correct; if that loop takes two minutes because Docker and a database have to come up, the loop breaks and the agent starts guessing instead of checking. A unit test is fast and needs nobody else, so each lane verifies itself without waiting for the one next door. The backend and the web being able to test R2 without talking to each other is exactly what lets them run in parallel.

And to a defined pattern, which is the part most often neglected. If you let each test be born however it comes out, in a month you have three repos with three styles, and inside each one as many styles as there were sessions. The agent has no opinion of its own about this: it writes the way you taught it, and if you didn't teach it, it writes however it feels that day. So the shape is equipped up front too:

items: **A testing skill per stack**, saying how testing actually works there: `angular-testing` for the web — TestBed, components with signals, how to fake an HTTP response — `flutter-testing` for mobile — widget tests, how to pump the tree — and the Nest best practices for the backend. Not generic testing theory: the idiom of each stack.
**One test, one behaviour.** If a test checks three things and fails, you have to read the whole thing to find out which one broke. If it checks one, the test name already told you.
**The name traced to the requirement.** The test for R2 says R2. That keeps `grep R2` working across all three repos, and it tells me which requirement was left uncovered when one is missing.

**No mocking the thing under test.** You fake what's outside — the network, the clock, storage — never the logic being tested. It's a model's favourite shortcut when a test resists: mock precisely the piece it was supposed to verify and call it green.
**And the mutation threshold as the closer**, because everything above can be followed to the letter and still leave you with tests that check nothing.

en.text: That last point is what keeps the standard from being decorative. The four rules above are about form, and form can be faked. Mutants are about substance: they change the code and ask whether anybody noticed. It's the difference between reviewing that a test is well written and checking that it's good for anything.
The tests: the same R# in three languages

This is where the contract stops being documentation and starts defending you. Because the requirement identifiers are the same in all three repos, one requirement turns into three tests talking about the same thing from three different places. Take R2 — the order was already cancelled, respond 409 and don't touch the inventory — and look at how it's tested in each lane:

items: On the backend, R2 is an endpoint test: I call the cancellation twice, require a 409 on the second, and check the inventory didn't move.
On the web, R2 is a screen test: I simulate the 409 the contract describes and require the right notice to appear and the button to be disabled.
On mobile, R2 is a widget test: the same simulated 409, the same notice, plus a double tap not firing two requests.
All three fail first. The contract doesn't exempt you from TDD: it gives the test something to fail against that isn't my intuition or what the backend did yesterday.

lines: # same bar in all three, a different tool per language
app/   dart run mutation_test   (mutation_test, from pub.dev)
→ target in all three: ≥ 80% of mutants killed
→ if a lane drops below the threshold, that task isn't done

en.caption: One requirement written once, tested in three languages. The tool that kills the mutants changes; the bar and the identifier don't.

en.text: Mutation testing is the step most people skip and the only one that tells you whether your tests are worth anything. The idea is old and simple: you change a line of code on purpose — a `>` for a `>=`, a `true` for a `false` — and run the suite again. If the tests stay green, that test wasn't proving anything: it was only passing. The tool changes with the language — Stryker in the two TypeScript lanes, `mutation_test` in Dart — but the bar doesn't. The same 80% in all three, because test quality can't depend on which repo you happened to land in.
I give an objective; the loop does the rest

Put in one sentence, my job in all of this is to give an objective. I don't dictate steps or review line by line while it writes: I hand over a user story turned into a contract and specs, and from there the orchestrator plans — reads the plan, looks at the tasks, decides the order within its lane — and delegates what belongs to whom: this is the backend's, this the web's, this mobile's. I show up at the end of each task, not in the middle.

What keeps that from turning into a disaster is where the tests sit, and I think it's the most useful idea in this whole note: **a test is the relationship between the criterion and the code.** The criterion lives in the spec, written in EARS with its R#. The code lives in the repo. The test is the only thing touching both at once that can say whether they match. Without it, the spec is an intention and the code is a promise, and nobody has ever held one up against the other.
The specification says what must happen. The code says what happens. The test is the only thing that looks at both and answers whether they are the same thing.

With that in place, the agent enters a loop that closes on its own: it writes against the spec, runs the tests, and if one fails, the code is broken — not "nearly right" — so it corrects and runs again. It repeats until the task satisfies what the requirement asked for. It doesn't move on because it believes it's done: it moves on because something outside it said so.

This is, plainly, the reason I found for why in practice I barely fight with hallucinations. And I want to say it carefully, because the easy version would be "this makes the model stop inventing", and that isn't true: **the model still invents.** What changes is that what it invents doesn't survive. A field that doesn't exist, an endpoint it imagined, a signature it remembered from another version: all of it crashes into a failing test one second later, inside the loop, and gets corrected before it reaches me. The invention doesn't disappear; it stops having an exit.
I didn't make the model stop being wrong. I made being wrong have immediate, automatic consequences, instead of showing up three days later on a user's screen.
Context: little and good, and let it think

The other half is missing, and it's the one most people get backwards. I don't hand the agent thousand-line files "just in case". I never give it all three repos, nor the whole `architecture.md`, nor the entire feature spec when it's on one specific task. I give it its contract, its spec, the skill that applies to what it's about to touch, and the README of the folder it's going to write in. Little, and chosen.

For a long time I thought that was just me being stingy with tokens. It turns out there's a better reason and it's documented. In [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), Anthropic's Applied AI team puts it this way: models have a finite "attention budget", and as the number of tokens in the context window grows, the model's ability to accurately recall the information inside it **decreases**. It isn't a cliff, it's a gradient: it still works with long contexts, but it loses precision at retrieving facts and at reasoning across things far apart from each other.
Finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome.
en.source: Anthropic's Applied AI Team · Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025

en.text: That principle names exactly why everything above is split the way it is. The contract in its own file and not inside the spec. The rules spread per folder instead of one four-hundred-line document. Skills that open only when the task needs them. A lane that never sees the other two repos. It isn't tidiness for its own sake: it's not spending its attention budget on things it won't use. The same article calls it "just-in-time" retrieval: the agent keeps lightweight references — file paths, links — and loads what it needs at the moment, instead of swallowing everything up front.

And here comes the part I find counter-intuitive, and that changed how I work: if I give it little context, what I do give it is time to think. When Anthropic introduced extended thinking in Claude 3.7 Sonnet, they published [an observation you can measure](https://www.anthropic.com/news/visible-extended-thinking): accuracy on maths questions **improves logarithmically with the number of thinking tokens** it is allowed to sample. Logarithmically means it genuinely goes up, though each step costs more than the last: the first push of reasoning buys a lot, the next one somewhat less, and so on. With a 64k thinking budget and parallel sampling they reached 84.8% on GPQA, with 96.5% on the physics portion.

The two together give me the rule I keep, and it's the exact opposite of what most people do: **little context and a lot of thinking.** The usual approach is the reverse — dump the whole repository in and ask for the answer now — and that loses on both sides: the excess context thins out its attention, and the rush strips away the reasoning steps that are precisely the ones that pay. I'd rather it read three files and think it over than read thirty and answer fast.
The third lane comes in through the front door

When I started writing this note, the mobile lane was the seam in the setup: `chalc feature` wired two paths — the web and the backend — and mobile was something I brought in by hand, copying the contract into the Flutter repo and generating its spec separately. It worked, but it skipped the sealing: if the contract changed, on mobile it was on me to remember. Writing it down here forced me to look the gap in the face, and it no longer exists: mobile comes in through the same command as the other two.

lines: ✓ Front: Angular  ·  Back: NestJS  ·  Mobile: Flutter
⠋ Orchestrating: contract → back spec → front spec → mobile spec
Shared contract in each spec: contracts/api.md

en.text: Mobile is a third consumer, with its `--mobile` flag or an interactive question: "Does the feature have a mobile app?". And it gets exactly the same treatment as the other two: its stack is detected, its skills are equipped, its spec comes out with its own MOBILE role — screens, navigation, connectivity, consuming the contract, with the order not to reimplement backend logic nor duplicate the frontend's — it shares the same number and the same R#, carries the stamped fingerprint and its `contract.lock.json`, and the branch is created in all three repos or in none.

There's a detail of the contract I care about more than the command: the contract is generated ONCE, knowing a mobile client exists. And when there isn't one, the prompt says so explicitly — "(no mobile app)" — so the model doesn't invent clients nobody asked for. It's the same rule as always, the no-padding rule, applied to an entire lane.

And the other seam closed the same way: Codex is now one more target in the catalog, alongside Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor and Gemini CLI. Its adapter writes the repo's `AGENTS.md` and its MCP servers in `.codex/config.toml`, with the same skills and the same method as the rest. The mobile repo's `AGENTS.md` stopped being maintained by hand: it comes out of the catalog, like everything else.
What actually improves

items: Integration day stops being an event. If all three honored the same contract, connecting is boring — and boring is exactly what you want it to be.
A change to R2 takes a second to find: `grep R2` across the three repos and there's everything to touch — contract, spec, tasks and tests, in backend, web and mobile.
No lane inherits decisions made in a chat it wasn't part of.
Each agent works with its own stack's rules and the same shared standard, so the code in all three repos looks like the house style and not like the model's mood that day.
And when I change tools in one lane — or try another, which is what I'm doing right now — nothing falls over: what rules is the contract, not who wrote the code.

Further reading

items: [chalc — the repository](https://github.com/ChristianCruzArango/chalc-cli-adapter): the CLI all of this comes from. The contract → back → front chaining lives in `lib/featureorch.mjs`, the hand-off in `lib/commands/feature.mjs`, the per-stack rules in `rules/` and each assistant's adapter in `targets/` — reading those three folders explains the whole distribution.

[EARS notation](https://alistairmavin.com/ears/) — Mav and colleagues at Rolls-Royce, 2009. Six patterns for writing requirements that can become tests; the contract uses the event-driven one, `WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …`, and that's what lets a single R# be tested in three languages.

[Contract Test](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContractTest.html) — Martin Fowler, 2011. Why a test against the contract warns you when the provider changes, instead of finding out in production. With three consumers instead of one, this weighs three times as much.

[Stryker Mutator](https://stryker-mutator.io/): the mutation testing engine for the two TypeScript lanes. You plug in a different runner depending on the test framework each repo already has, so there's no separate suite to build.

[mutation_test](https://pub.dev/packages/mutation_test): the Dart equivalent, on pub.dev. Same idea — change the code on purpose and see whether the tests notice — as a command line tool with configurable mutation rules.

[Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli): the official documentation, including how `AGENTS.md` hands Codex the project instructions. It's the equivalent of the `CLAUDE.md` I was already using in the other two repos, which is why splitting by lanes forces no change to the method.
[Angular CLI MCP Server](https://angular.dev/ai/mcp): how to start it and which tools it exposes. It's what equips the web lane so it consults today's version instead of the one the model remembers.

[Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents) — Anthropic Applied AI team, 2025. The attention budget, why accuracy drops as the context window fills, and the principle of finding the smallest set of high-signal tokens. The best explanation of why I split the rules up instead of piling them together.

[Claude's extended thinking](https://www.anthropic.com/news/visible-extended-thinking) — Anthropic, 2025. Where they publish that accuracy improves logarithmically with thinking tokens, and how a thinking budget is set. The half that pays off for giving little context.
